pmi.summary: Conventional PMI pricing and cancellation are separate questions. Original loan-to-value determines the illustrative premium; the original-value 80% request, original-schedule 78% automatic termination and month-after-midpoint rule determine distinct potential ending dates.
pmi.scope: U.S. borrower-paid monthly conventional PMI on unmodified, fully amortizing fixed-rate principal-residence loans closed on or after July 29, 1999. It excludes FHA MIP, VA, lender-paid insurance, high-risk exceptions and investor-specific appreciation rules. Rates from a dated insurer card are illustrations, not quotes.

examples.title: A quoted PMI premium with zero interest
examples.inputs: Purchase and original value $200,000; 10% down; quoted annual PMI 0.5%; zero interest; 30 years; no extra principal.
steps: Original loan = 200,000 × 90% = 180,000; original LTV = 90%.
Monthly P&I = 180,000 / 360 = 500. After payment 40 the balance is 160,000, the 80% request threshold.
This model charges through the qualifying request payment, then stops after assumed approval. Scheduled 78% termination has a separate due-date convention.
examples.answer: Initial monthly PMI is $75; an 80% request requires borrower action and all conditions.

examples.title: A low current LTV does not prove PMI has ended
examples.inputs: Original value $400,000; original loan $380,000; current balance $320,000; current home value $500,000; ten payments completed.
steps: Current-market LTV = 320,000 / 500,000 = 64%.
Original-value LTV = 320,000 / 400,000 = 80%.
The 80% request threshold is met, but payment history, liens, value evidence and written approval still need confirmation.
The scheduled 78% date remains tied to the original amortization, so an entered $150 premium is not silently removed just because the balance is now at 80%.
examples.answer: The modeled current quote remains $150 while the request is unapproved.

questions.question: Does PMI automatically stop at 80% LTV?
questions.answer: No. At 80% of original value you may request cancellation in writing, subject to current payments, good history, no junior liens and value evidence. Automatic termination generally uses scheduled 78%, with a midpoint backstop if current.

questions.question: Can a higher current appraisal remove PMI?
questions.answer: It can matter under investor-specific appreciation rules, which may require seasoning and a new appraisal. This calculator reports current-value LTV separately and does not substitute it for original value under the HPA rules.

questions.question: Do extra payments move the automatic 78% date?
questions.answer: They can move the actual 80% request threshold forward. The statutory scheduled 78% date is based on the original amortization; an early payoff separately ends the loan.

questions.question: What if payments are past due?
questions.answer: Automatic and midpoint termination require current payments. The existing-loan mode keeps the quoted premium active when payments are not current and does not invent a catch-up or cancellation date.

questions.question: Are these FHA MIP or government PMI rates?
questions.answer: No. FHA has separate MIP rules. The estimate uses a dated National MI conventional base-rate card with stated coverage assumptions. Use My Quote for your actual annual rate, or FHA Loan Calculator for FHA insurance.

biweekly-mortgage.summary: Paying half a monthly payment every two weeks produces 26 half-payments, equal to 13 monthly payments per modeled year. The calculator compares this with ordinary monthly payments and with a monthly plan that has the same annual outlay.
biweekly-mortgage.scope: Fixed nominal-rate P&I with equal 1/26-year periods and immediate crediting of each payment. This is not twice-monthly payment, an exact 14-day daily-interest calendar, or a lender holding-account simulation. Taxes, insurance, PMI, fees and penalties are excluded.

examples.title: An extra annual payment without interest
examples.inputs: $12,000 principal, zero interest, 12 months remaining, no extra payment above the half-monthly amount.
steps: Monthly payment = 12,000 / 12 = 1,000.
Biweekly payment = 1,000 / 2 = 500; a full-year budget is 500 × 26 = 13,000.
Only 24 payments of $500 are needed to repay $12,000.
There is no interest saving at 0%, even though the modeled loan is repaid earlier.
examples.answer: Biweekly payment is $500, with 24 actual payments and zero interest.

examples.title: Same annual budget, monthly alternative
steps: The biweekly annual budget is $13,000.
A matched monthly plan pays 13,000 / 12 = 1,083.333333 per month.
Both plans pay extra relative to $1,000 per month; the different period lengths affect the actual last payment.
examples.answer: The matched-budget monthly amount is about $1,083.33.

expected.label: Monthly payment with the same annual budget

questions.question: Is biweekly the same as twice a month?
questions.answer: No. Biweekly is modeled as 26 payments per year; semimonthly is 24. The extra two half-payments account for a large part of accelerated payoff.

questions.question: Will my servicer immediately credit each half-payment?
questions.answer: Not necessarily. Ask how partial payments are applied and whether there are fees. Holding two halves until the monthly due date changes the timing benefit.

questions.question: Why include an equal-budget monthly comparison?
questions.answer: It separates paying extra from paying earlier. A monthly extra-principal plan can reproduce much of the saving without enrolling in a biweekly service.

questions.question: Does this use actual 14-day payment dates?
questions.answer: No. It uses annual nominal rate divided by 26 and equal modeled periods. Real daily accrual, calendar alignment and years with 27 pay dates require the lender’s actual convention.

questions.question: How do I use the biweekly mortgage calculator with extra payments?
questions.answer: Enter extra principal in Extra per biweekly payment. This amount is added to each half-monthly payment, not once per month: $100 extra means $2,600 over 26 modeled payments in a full year. Compare both ordinary monthly payments and the equal-budget monthly alternative; actual total extra paid ends when the loan is repaid. Confirm that your servicer applies extra funds to principal and credits partial payments as assumed.

sources.title: FNCalculator: dedicated biweekly payment comparison inputs
CFPB: mortgage principal and interest amortization

discount-points.summary: Compare two fixed-rate loan quotes with the same principal and term. Points cost 1% of principal per point, but the rate reduction must come from the lender’s actual quote. The comparison distinguishes monthly cash savings from interest-and-fee savings at a sale or refinancing horizon.
discount-points.scope: Cash-paid points and entered upfront costs on same-principal, same-term fixed-rate quotes. Negative points represent an entered lender credit. No financed fees, tax deduction, discounting, ownership-cost difference, PMI or prepayment penalty is inferred.

examples.title: One point costs one percent, not a promised rate reduction
examples.inputs: $100,000 principal; A quoted at 6% with no points; B quoted at 5.75% with one point. Both quotes are entered assumptions.
steps: Offer B point cost = 100,000 × 1% = 1,000.
Each monthly payment is calculated from its own quoted rate over 360 months.
The rate reduction is not generated from the number of points: the lender must quote both.
At sale or refinancing compare interest plus upfront costs, not only the difference in payments.
examples.answer: One point costs $1,000 on this loan; the break-even depends on the quoted rates and holding period.

expected.label: Offer B points or credit amount

examples.title: Points with no rate benefit never recover their cost
examples.inputs: Both loans are $12,000 for two years at 0%; only offer B charges one point.
steps: Both monthly payments are 12,000 / 24 = 500.
Offer B costs an extra 12,000 × 1% = 120 upfront.
There is no interest or payment saving to offset the extra cost.
examples.answer: B is $120 more expensive at the selected horizon; no break-even is reached within the term.

expected.label: Net borrowing-cost savings at horizon (B vs A)

questions.question: Does one point always reduce my rate by 0.25%?
questions.answer: No. One point describes a fee equal to 1% of principal. The lender, loan type and market determine the quoted rate change.

questions.question: Why are cash-flow and borrowing-cost break-even different?
questions.answer: Payment savings exclude differences in principal repaid. Borrowing-cost savings compare interest and upfront costs, equivalently including the remaining-balance advantage at sale or refinancing.

questions.question: What holding period should I use?
questions.answer: Use the expected time before selling, refinancing or paying off the loan, and compare shorter and longer alternatives. Zero months compares upfront costs only.

questions.question: Can I enter lender credits?
questions.answer: Yes. Negative points are treated as a cash credit at closing. A higher-rate quote can start ahead and later become more costly; first break-even is not a promise of a permanent advantage.

questions.question: Are taxes or financed points included?
questions.answer: No. Points and entered other fees are paid in cash. Tax deductibility, financed closing costs and the opportunity cost of cash need a different analysis.

questions.question: Is a mortgage points calculator the same as a discount points calculator?
questions.answer: Here both names mean comparing upfront discount points against the interest rate in each lender quote. Enter points and other upfront costs separately for offers A and B. Origination fees do not automatically buy a lower rate, and this model does not infer a rate reduction from the number of points. Compare the net borrowing cost at your expected sale or refinance date as well as monthly payment savings.

sources.title: CFPB: discount points, lender credits and lender-specific rate changes
